source.title: Efficient Refusal Ablation in LLM through Optimal Transport
source.authors: Géraldin Nanfack; Eugene Belilovsky; Elvis Dohmatob

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates the original difference-in-means refusal feature ablation (RFA): it extracts the harmful-minus-harmless direction and projects it out across layers, then reports harmful-output attack success. It also compares that intervention with a different distribution-matching intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own RFA baseline results, PCA-OT attack results, layer-sensitivity results, and capability measurements. Hyperparameter-selection values and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs the original difference-in-means refusal feature ablation (RFA, projected out at all layers) on six chat/instruct models and reports HarmBench LlamaGuard ASR and perplexity. This bears on V1. Its main contribution is a distribution-matching affine intervention (PCA-Gaussian OT), argued explicitly against the 'restrictive' one-dimensional account. That argument bears on V4 through the affine/distributional framing. The PCA-OT comparisons are partly own-method-vs-baseline performance, so V4 evidence is indirect.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim Gaussian OT over a PCA subspace beats single-direction projection, by up to ~11% ASR at comparable perplexity. They say refusal is localized to 40–60% depth rather than distributed across layers, and that alignment is vulnerable beyond direction removal. They also note Qwen2.5-32B is more resistant, which they suggest reflects scale, and that gains on Qwen are inconsistent for one-layer OT.
record.recipe_differences: The RFA comparator uses the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and all-layer projection. The proposed primary method instead maps harmful activation distributions toward harmless ones using PCA and Gaussian optimal transport, usually at one or two selected layers.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model, intervention layer/depth, number of PCA components, and number of intervention layers. The reported layer sweeps show distinct layer profiles for Llama-2-13B and Qwen2.5-14B; two-layer interventions can outperform one-layer interventions, but sometimes worsen perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA-OT effectiveness is localized: shallow layers give ASR <5%, middle layers (40–60% depth) peak, and Qwen2.5-14B declines at deep layers; deep-layer high ASR in Llama is degenerate repetition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation interventions that bypass refusal are most effective at middle layers; deep-layer ASR can be spurious.

fits_no_version.finding: Capability and perplexity costs of the PCA-OT attack are model-dependent; GSM8K falls from 27.98 to 21.38 on Llama-2-13B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributional activation jailbreaks retain most benchmark ability but with task- and model-dependent costs.

record.problems: The paper reports ASR using a safety classifier and also notes that high ASR can be spurious when outputs collapse into repetition. The six-model main table reports means over 4 seeds, but the detailed layer-sensitivity tables give no uncertainty. Direct general-capability benchmark comparisons are reported only for Llama-2-13B and for PCA-OT, not for RFA.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted separate Table 1 Alpaca perplexity entries, AcT comparator results, detailed layer-sweep points beyond selected diagnostic layers, component-count ablations, category-specific attack rates, and qualitative example outputs. These were not needed to represent the tested versions within the 60-row limit; the recorded rows prioritize direct RFA outcomes, PCA-OT comparisons, capability checks, and layer-dependent findings.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. Capability benchmarks (MMLU etc.) after RFA; only perplexity is reported for RFA.
Cone or multi-direction accounts are not tested directly; no comparison with affine concept ablation or with refusal cones.
No weight edit or abliterated released model.
No analysis of other jailbreaks or of adversarial training.

missing.what: Layer-matched comparison on Llama-2-13B: RFA with the layer-24 direction 46.5% vs PCA-OT 75.5%; RFA with the layer-22 direction 26.4% vs PCA-OT 78.6% (Pile PPL 8.06–8.95)
Component count K: Llama-2-13B K=1 81.1%, K=2 82.4%, K=5 80.5%, K=10 76.1%; Qwen2.5-14B K=1 73.6%, K=5 81.8% with PPL rising to 132.9 at K=10
Geometric claim that RFA collapses variance along PC1 and does not overlap the harmless distribution
Alpaca perplexity for RFA (e.g. 4.89 vs 4.99 baseline on Llama-2-7B)

record.verdict_notes: RFA is run as a tuned baseline (direction layer chosen on validation, last-token extraction following Yu et al. 2025), with no system prompt. ASR is judged by LlamaGuard-2, so it measures harmful output rather than refusal per se. The text and Table 1 disagree on Qwen2.5-14B PCA-OT1 (69.81 vs 84.43). K=1 performing nearly as well as K=2 weakens a multi-direction reading of V4; the advantage looks like affine/variance matching at a chosen layer. Preprint; no code is stated.

versions.untested_parts: Tests removal with RFA and reports attack success; does not test adding the direction to induce refusals. Capability measurements for PCA-OT are not capability measurements after RFA.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested; interventions use inference-time activation hooks.
Does not test whether other attacks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.

Tests RFA against PCA-Gaussian OT, a distributional alternative, and reports layer and component sensitivity. Does not directly test affine, cone, or dominant-direction-plus-others models as competing mechanistic accounts.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.
Does not test reasoning models that reason before answering.

labels.reason: One-layer PCA-OT is below RFA on Qwen2.5-32B (45.75 vs 57.55), but two layers beat it, so the result depends on a method choice. Table 4's K=1≈K=2 is Llama-2-13B only. Table 6 shows K=5 raising ASR on Qwen2.5-14B (81.8 vs 73.6), so the reason's 'not extra directions' is overstated.

relation.reason: Its own RFA runs (with baselines and perplexity) bear on V1, and the RFA vs affine-OT comparison bears on V4.

tranche.reason: The study runs the original RFA (DIM direction, all-layer projection, chat template, no system prompt) and argues the one-dimensional framing is restrictive. Its affine OT map does better, and RFA is weak on Llama-2-13B and Qwen2.5-32B and depends on the extraction layer.

source_check.notes: For Qwen2.5-14B PCA-OT1, Table 1 and Sec 4.1 disagree (84.43 ± 3.45 vs 69.81, 'underperforms'). Llama-2-13B and Qwen2.5-14B PCA-OT2 both print 83.81 ± 0.16. RFA here is the authors' own run (last-token direction, following Yu et al. 2025). Capability benchmarks (Table 9) cover only PCA-OT1 on Llama-2-13B. RFA at layer 22 (26.4%, Table 2) has no row.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-14B PCA-OT1: Table 1 gives 84.43 ± 3.45, but the Sec 4.1 prose gives 69.81 vs RFA 79.45. Llama-3.1-8B PCA-OT1: 74.69 ± 1.42 vs RFA 72.69 ± 1.05. Qwen2.5-7B: 79.40 vs 77.94, which the paper calls 'marginal'. RFA projects at all layers, PCA-OT intervenes at 1–2. The layer-matched check (Table 2) covers only Llama-2-13B.
statements.problem: Every listed number is right, but the statement leaves out Qwen2.5-14B one-layer, where the prose says PCA-OT1 underperforms RFA. The one-layer gains on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B are small.

statements.correction: Table 4 (Llama-2-13B): K=1 81.1, K=2 82.4, K=5 80.5, K=10 76.1. Table 6 (Qwen2.5-14B): K=1 73.6, K=2 73.0, K=5 81.8 (Pile PPL 19.2 vs 7.21), K=10 67.3. There is no pure-translation arm.
statements.problem: The K=1 vs K=2 figures come from Llama-2-13B only. On Qwen2.5-14B, more components raise ASR, so 'not extra directions' does not hold in general. Mean shift and variance matching are never tested separately.
